newsitem.title: USA: Product intros hit record level, but not all new.
newsitem.headline: Product intros hit record level, but not all new.

text.p: Marketers introduced a record 24,496 products in 1996, but only 7.2 percent of those were really new, according to Marketing Intelligence Service Thursday.
The Naples, N.Y.-based new product tracking company said introductions of food, beverage, health & beauty, household and pet products rose 17.7 percent in 1996 from the previous year.

Nevertheless, products that were truly innovative, offering significant new or added benefits, increased only slightly, about half a percentage point, far below the peak innovation rate of 18.6 percent in 1986.

"New products are everywhere, but not many are outstanding and different," said Tom Vierhile, general manager of the firm. He said companies fear taking a risk on something really different, preferring instead to extend their own brand with a new flavor or other minor variation.
That may be short-sighted, Vierhile suggests.
"The No. 1 reason for product failure is the lack of a competitive point of difference," he said. "Yet, there are thousands of products introduced that lack an innovative point of difference."

He believes developing a product that's really different is worth the risk. "No one wants to have a failure," Vierhile said. "However, products that are really innovative have a better chance of hitting a home run."
Seeking to recognise and reward innovative products, Marketing Intelligence Service announced the following winners of its 1996 Build a Better Mousetrap award:

1. Pillsbury OneStep Ready to Bake pan cookie. More like a pizza than a cookie, this refrigerated dough is packaged in a round foil pan; from Pillsbury Co., the North American unit of Grand Metropolitan PLC.
2. Jell-O Stir Snack Instant Pudding Mix. Packed in a resealable canister with a measuring scoop, this pudding lets the consumer decide how many servings to make; from Kraft Foods Inc.
3. Colonial Toaster Magic Bread. Ready-to-toast bread with the toppings -- honey and butter or cinnamon and butter -- already spread; from Earthgrains Co., St. Louis.
4. State Fair Incredi-Bagel stuffed bagels. Bagels filled with ready-to-eat breakfast or lunch foods; from State Fair Foods, Dallas.

5. Stockpot Classic Soups concentrate. Sold in the refrigerated dairy case, these 10 oz. resealable pouches contain fresh-cut vegetables, real dairy products and premium meats and seafood; from Stockpot Soups, Redmond, Wash.
6. Hershey's Goodnight Kisses Hot Cocoa Mix and Goodnight Hugs Hot Cocoa Mix. Tiny Kisses and Hugs candies melt with the mix; from Hershey Foods Corp.
7. Windex NoDrip glass cleaner. This stays-where-you-spray-it cleaner eliminates drips; from S.C. Johnson & Son.
8. Instead 12-hour feminine protection cup. Worn internally, the cup has twice the wearing time of a tampon; from Ultrafem Inc., Missoula, Mt.
9. Children's Mylanta. The first upset stomach remedy for children aged 2 to 11; from Johnson & Johnson Merck Consumer Pharmaceuticals Co.
10. GladWare tight sealing containers. Inexpensive, resealable plastic containers in two sizes: soup & salad and entree; from First Brands Corp.

The top 10 U.S. new product innovations were ranked in the areas of formulation, positioning, packaging, technology or creating a new market. Winners were chosen by Marketing Intelligence Service from more than 24,000 new entries reported in 1996 in the firm's Product Alert publication. All were introduced nationally, regionally or in test markets in 1996.
